text: Hi, I have to add 1/4 and 2/3 and I don't get it.
Hi Maya! Great problem to practice. Before we add them, what do you notice about the bottom numbers — the denominators — of 1/4 and 2/3?
One is 4 and one is 3. So the answer is 3/7? I just added the tops and bottoms.

That's a really common idea, but adding the tops and bottoms separately changes the size of the pieces. The denominators have to match first. Think of it like adding quarters of a pizza to thirds of a pizza — the slices are different sizes. What number do both 4 and 3 divide into evenly?
Exactly, 12! So we rewrite both fractions with 12 on the bottom. 1/4 is how many twelfths? (Hint: 4 times what is 12?)
4 times 3 is 12, so 1/4 is 3/12. And 2/3 is... 3 times 4 is 12, so 8/12.
Perfect — you multiplied the top by the same number as the bottom, which keeps the value the same. Now the slices match. What is 3/12 + 8/12?
11/12! Do I add the bottoms this time too?

You've got 11/12 right! And good question — no. Once the denominators match, they stay the same; we only add the numerators, because we're just counting how many equal pieces we have. So 3 twelfths plus 8 twelfths is 11 twelfths.
Oh that makes sense now. Can I try 1/2 + 1/6 by myself?
Yes, go for it — I'd love to see your steps!
Common bottom is 6. 1/2 is 3/6. 3/6 + 1/6 = 4/6. That's the answer.
Beautiful work, and your method is spot on! One last challenge: 4/6 can be simplified. Do 4 and 6 share a common factor you could divide out?
They both divide by 2, so 2/3. Thanks, this is way less scary now.
2/3 — exactly right, and well spotted. You went from adding tops and bottoms to finding common denominators and simplifying in one session. That's real progress, Maya!
